title: China to ASEAN: Promote peace, trust despite tensions
summary: Pointing out that “flame runs high when everyone adds wood to the fire,” a ranking Chinese official yesterday called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to promote peace and…

blocks.text: President Marcos joins hands with other ASEAN leaders plus South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and Chinese Premier Li Qiang on November 17, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Pointing out that “flame runs high when everyone adds wood to the fire,” a ranking Chinese official yesterday called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to promote peace and mutual trust as tensions over the the South China Sea simmer.

Chinese Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs Zhang Zhu cited the need for parties to “fend off risks and challenges together,” accelerate regional integration and “inject more positive energy to stability and prosperity” in the region and beyond.

“The more difficulties we face, the more unity and coordination we need. The foundation of cooperation is mutual trust,” Zhang said during the 29th ASEAN-Plus Three Summit. ASEAN-Plus comprises the members of the regional bloc as well as Japan, South Korea and China.

“Countries in the region should do more things that would contribute to mutual trust and regional peace and stability. Shoulder more sense of responsibility other than geopolitical calculations. Only in this way can we harness the role of ASEAN-Plus Three cooperation as a main channel of East Asian cooperation,” he added.

Zhang made the remark as Filipino and Chinese officials engage in ugly public exchanges over Beijing’s illegal claim over the West Philippine Sea, the part of the South China Sea within the Philippines’ 200-nautical mile exclusive economic zone and continental shelf.
Philippine officials have denounced Chinese acts of provocations at sea, but Beijing dismissed the allegations as exaggerations.
China claims virtually the entire South China Sea, which serves as the passageway to more than 60 percent of global trade.
The other claimants are Taiwan and ASEAN members Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.
ASEAN and China signed a non-legally binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea in 2002 to prevent tensions from escalating and maintain stability in the region.

However, legally binding rules have yet to be completed and approved. Officials have admitted that the code of conduct would not be finished within the period of Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN Summit this year.
In 2016, an arbitral tribunal based in The Hague invalidated China’s wide-reaching maritime claim, but the Chinese government refused to recognize the landmark decision.
In his opening remarks for the ASEAN-Plus Three Summit, President Marcos called for joint efforts to ensure that existing commitments would be felt by citizens.

“As we approach 30 years of ASEAN-Plus Three cooperation, let us renew our ambition for this partnership and shorten the distance between the commitments we make around this table and the benefits our peoples feel in their daily lives,” he added.
